info.bio:
En el origen del techno, no solo en su nacimiento sino también en el momento exacto de su gestación, está Cybotron. Formado en Detroit, ciudad que da a luz este sonido, se trata de un grupo de electro con rasgos comunes a otros de la época pero cuya aproximación destaca por la abstracción y su sonoridad por los matices oscuros y futuristas. 

Desde su primera producción en 1981 no dejan de alejarse del hip hop al que se asocian los grupos de electro de Nueva York.

own_scenes.family: Los pioneros: Atkins, May, Saunderson y la primera ola
own_scenes.desc: Juan Atkins, hijo del este de Detroit trasladado a Belleville, donde una clase de «estudios del futuro» le descubrió a Alvin Toffler, conoció en el Washtenaw Community College a Richard «Rik» Davis, veterano de Vietnam, músico electrónico de montaje abstracto, místico y secretista, que se hacía llamar «3070». Juntos inventaron «the grid», un diccionario de palabras compuestas para el futuro; de él salió «cybotron» (cyborg + ciclotrón). Más turbio y sombrío que Kraftwerk, al que Atkins dice que no conocía cuando empezó con los sintetizadores, y psicodélico por herencia de Parliament-Funkadelic y Bernie Worrell. «Alleys of Your Mind» (1981), una cancioncilla sobre la paranoia y el control mental grabada en cuatro pistas, rescató el funk de las bandas de veinte músicos y los pañales gigantes; con el apoyo de The Electrifying Mojo, ella y «Cosmic Cars» vendieron decenas de miles de copias en el sello Deep Space antes de que Fantasy, el sello de Brubeck en Berkeley, les mandara un contrato por correo. Un año antes que «Planet Rock», pero introvertido. Enter (1983), casi rock progresivo contra el complejo militar-industrial, lleva escondido el código genético del techno; «Clear», remezclada por Jose «Animal» Diaz, estuvo nueve semanas en la lista negra de Billboard y demostró que la electrónica podía tener soul. Davis quería ir hacia el rock y Atkins no quería «Techno City» tras «Clear»: se separaron en 1984-1985. Nunca tocaron en un bar.

refs.q: Moreover, Cybotron helped make funk palatable and relevant again, rescuing it from the grandiosity of eleven-, twelve-, and twenty-piece bands, fright wigs, giant diapers, and elaborate stage sets—all with a little ditty about paranoia and thought control, recorded on a four-track tape machine.
refs.para: Cybotron’s first single, “Alleys of Your Mind,” was released in 1981, apparently just after the landmark “Sharevari.” Though it wasn’t the first “techno” record to come out of Detroit, it became a much bigger success, proving that Cybotron’s economy of language had more staying power than A Number of Names. Whereas “Sharevari” was a more direct extension of the music popular in the northwest side, “Alleys” reconnected those influences with the bedrock of funk that will always be a part of Detroit. Moreover, Cybotron helped make funk palatable and relevant again, rescuing it from the grandiosity of eleven-, twelve-, and twenty-piece bands, fright wigs, giant diapers, and elaborate stage sets—all with a little ditty about paranoia and thought control, recorded on a four-track tape machine.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: We didn’t know anything about [Fantasy’s interest] until one day we opened the mailbox and found a contract.”
refs.para: “[Our second record was] being distributed by a local distributor [AMI],” Atkins remembers. “We were selling so many records that Bob Schwartz [the distributor] called up the independent distributor for Fantasy [Records].” This was a rather strange way to go about getting a record deal, especially since Cybotron certainly wasn’t waiting for any A&R scouts to come knocking. Instead, Atkins had transformed Deep Space, his former DJ collective, into a label and publishing company for the group’s records. “We weren’t ‘discovered,’” says Atkins. “We sold our own records on Deep Space—10,000 copies of ‘Alleys of Your Mind’ and 10,000–15,000 of ‘Cosmic Cars’—before Fantasy even realized who we were. We didn’t know anything about [Fantasy’s interest] until one day we opened the mailbox and found a contract.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: And contrary to what soul music purists had claimed, “Clear” proved that electronic music could have soul.
refs.para: Adding to the impact of Enter, the single “Clear” made a huge splash and became Cybotron’s biggest hit, especially after it was remixed by Jose “Animal” Diaz. “Clear” climbed the charts in Dallas, Houston, and Miami, and spent nine weeks on the Billboard Top Black Singles chart (as it was called then) in fall 1983, peaking at No. 52. “Clear” was a success. And contrary to what soul music purists had claimed, “Clear” proved that electronic music could have soul. In other words, Atkins and Davis drew a new line in the definition of electronic music styles, representing a milestone in the fusion of electronic experimentation with funky dance music.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: I mean, we had black radio programmers eating out of our hands!”
refs.para: At the peak of Cybotron’s success in 1983 and 1984, a difference in direction caused Atkins to set out on his own. Davis wanted to take the group’s sound in a more rock-based direction and, what’s more, the difference between “Clear” and its follow-up, “Techno City,” was too great for Atkins: “I was against that record [‘Techno City’]. It’s a great record, but it wasn’t the right one to follow ‘Clear.’ I mean, we had black radio programmers eating out of our hands!” With the national impact of “Clear,” techno might have developed quite differently had Cybotron stayed in the game.

scenes.name: Techno de Detroit
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El techno sale de Detroit casi sin que nadie lo note, pero Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson y Carl Craig cambiarán las discotecas del mundo. Atkins acuña el término para el funk de alta tecnología de Cybotron y quiere casar el funk abstracto de Parliament con el synth-pop robótico de Kraftwerk (Model 500, «No UFO's»); Saunderson lanza el boom de 1988 con Inner City; May («el Miles Davis del techno») firma «Strings Of Life»; Carl Craig lo lleva lejos de la pista (Landcruising).

scenes.name: El techno de Detroit
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: La tesis del libro: el techno no nació en Europa ni es un apéndice del house de Chicago, sino de Detroit, incubadora de una música que tuvo que irse fuera (Reino Unido, Alemania) para tener el impacto que merecía. Brewster recuerda que la primera edición (1999) le devolvió la historia a la ciudad, con sus DJs (The Electrifying Mojo, Ken Collier, The Wizard, Richard Davis), sus fiestas de instituto, sus pitidos electrónicos y su dudosa moda italiana, un mundo aparte de Nueva York o Los Ángeles. Esta segunda edición (2010) amplía la historia de Detroit: cómo The Wizard se convirtió en Jeff Mills, Ann Arbor («el hermano pequeño y empollón» de Detroit), la WCBN y Ghostly, la escena de fiestas de mediados de los noventa, el festival de Hart Plaza y la emigración a Berlín. Sicko deja fuera adrede el rave y el éxtasis, y los esquemas de sintetizadores: lo que define el techno es más la ciudad que las máquinas.

podcast.title: Afrofuturist Sound Impact
podcast.body: The Afrofuturist sound developed by Cybotron gained significant traction among Detroit's youth, contributing to the emergence of a new musical scene in the city. "El sonido de Afrofuturista, DitiBotron estaba llegando fuerte a la juventud de Detroit, y se estaba creando una escena."

podcast.title: Detroit Techno Influence
podcast.body: Cybotron's music, specifically the track "Zohyfield of Demoroder" (as transcribed, likely a mis-transcription for "Clear"), was a significant influence in Detroit during the genesis of techno, alongside Kraftwerk. "lo que más escuchaba era Crafwerk, junto al tema Zohyfield of Demoroder."

srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Formation and Shared Interests
podcast.body: Formed in 1980 by Juan Atkins and Richard Davis, whom Atkins met while studying music. Davis, a Vietnam veteran, was considerably older than Atkins. They connected through mutual interests in science fiction, futurism, and electronic music. "En 1980 forma a Cibotron, junto a Richard Davis... Ambos eran la ficionadas a la fíjana ficción, a los futuros logos y a la música electrónica."

srcs.episode: Cómo Detroit Reinventó la Música Electrónica ｜ Pioneros del Techno

podcast.title: Musical Divergence and Split
podcast.body: Although they shared common ground, their individual musical preferences led to the group's separation in the mid-1980s. Richard Davis desired a shift towards rock music, while Atkins was committed to continuing the electronic path that was proving successful. "Mediados de los 80, Cibo Tron se separó, y a que Richard Davis quería dar un giro hacia el rock, y Atkins quería seguir el camino electrónico que tanto les estaba funcionando."

srcs.episode: Cómo Detroit Reinventó la Música Electrónica ｜ Pioneros del Techno

podcast.title: Seminal Techno Project
podcast.body: Early tracks from Cybotron, a seminal techno project, are characterized as a blend of American funk and the technological minimalism of Kraftwerk, showcasing the foundational influences of the genre. "Las primeros tracks de Cibo Tron o model 500, proyectos seminales del tecno, son como un hijo bastardo de ese fancaamericano y del minimalismo tecnológico de Crafwerk."
